## ABSTRACT

Pulmonary embolism (PE) has a significant impact on right-sided heart function. Clinical presentation can range from no involvement of the right ventricle to right ventricular dysfunction, cardiogenic shock, and even cardiac arrest. The authors explore the pathophysiology of PE-induced right ventricular failure, emphasizing the mechanisms by which PE contributes to dysfunction, current diagnostic tools for risk stratification, and the importance of timely diagnosis. The primary focus is on strategies for managing right ventricular failure secondary to PE, including medical, percutaneous interventional, and surgical options. Recent advances in the field are also noted, including emerging therapies and evolving treatment algorithms.

KEY POINTS

* Inpatient mortality for patients with high-risk PE is as high as 42.1% and is primarily due to right ventricular dysfunction from a sudden rise in right ventricular afterload.
* Risk of mortality is classified as low, intermediate (intermediate low-risk and intermediate high-risk), and high.
* Management of PE with right ventricular involvement of varying severity requires prompt and concomitant integration of several approaches: management of hemodynamics (preload and afterload), reperfusion, pharmacologic support, supportive care, and, in refractory cases, use of mechanical circulatory support and advanced therapy.

Pulmonary embolism (PE) significantly impacts right-sided heart function. Clinical presentation can range from no involvement of the right ventricle to right ventricular dysfunction, cardiogenic shock, and even cardiac arrest. In a retrospective subset from the Pulmonary Embolism Response Team Consortium Registry,[1](#ref-1) inpatient mortality was as high as 42.1% in patients with high-risk PE with hemodynamic collapse (termed *catastrophic* PE). Management requires critical evaluation, risk stratification, and multidisciplinary care that can include medical, percutaneous interventional, and surgical options. This article predominantly discusses patients classified as having intermediate- and high-risk PE, given the associated hemodynamics and involvement of the right ventricle.

## RIGHT VENTRICULAR FAILURE IN ACUTE PE

Acute PE is associated with an elevated risk of death, primarily due to acute right ventricular dysfunction resulting from a sudden rise in right ventricular afterload.[2](#ref-2) Vascular obstruction caused by thrombus in the pulmonary arterial circulation can lead to significant increases in pulmonary pressures and pulmonary vascular resistance, raising right ventricular afterload. In PE, hypoxemia and pulmonary vasoconstrictors also contribute to pulmonary vascular resistance. The crescent-shaped right ventricle, characterized by fine layers of myofibrils arranged in series for volume expansion and enhanced compliance compared with the left ventricle, is designed to tolerate preload changes and is compliant in low-pressure systems. It struggles to adapt rapidly to acute elevations in circulatory pressures and has limited capacity to adapt to sudden increases in afterload.

During an acute PE, the right ventricle attempts to preserve right ventricle–pulmonary artery coupling and maintain stroke volume and cardiac output by dilating and altering its geometry.[3](#ref-3) However, the right ventricle cannot endure consistently elevated pressures, which leads to further right ventricular dilation and acute septal deviation toward the left ventricle, giving rise to altered ventricular interdependence—a phenomenon where the performance of one ventricle is influenced by the other due to the shared interventricular septum. Consequently, the right ventricle exerts pressure on the interventricular septum, impairing filling of the left ventricle, decreasing left ventricular preload, and reducing blood supply to the coronary arteries.

The increase in right ventricular intramural pressure and wall tension also causes straightening of the wall of the right ventricle, leading to decreased right coronary artery perfusion and right ventricular ischemia, even in individuals without preexisting coronary disease.[2](#ref-2) Furthermore, with persistent right ventricular dilation and enlargement, the tricuspid valve annulus may expand, resulting in inadequate closure of the valve leaflets and subsequent secondary tricuspid regurgitation. These effects create a cycle of ischemia, compounded by decreased oxygenation from obstructive thrombotic material, resulting in a drop in blood pressure and hemodynamic changes, all of which may manifest as syncope, hypotension, cardiogenic shock, and cardiac arrest ([Figure 1](#F1)).[2](#ref-2),[4](#ref-4) Moreover, this dysfunction permits retrograde blood flow into the right atrium, compromising right ventricular filling, elevating right atrial pressure, and contributing to progressive venous congestion.

## DIAGNOSTIC AND PROGNOSTIC TOOLS IN ACUTE PE

Signs of right ventricular involvement can be observed through laboratory and imaging studies. Computed tomography pulmonary angiography has been a cornerstone in the diagnosis of acute PE due to its detailed contrast enhancement of pulmonary vasculature. It is also a valuable tool in assessment of the right ventricle. Per the 2019 European Respiratory Society (ERS) guidelines, an increase in the right ventricle-to-left ventricle diameter ratio greater than 1 found with computed tomography pulmonary angiography ([Figure 2](#F2)) is indicative of acute right ventricular dysfunction, and is associated with increased risk of adverse outcomes and all-cause and PE-related mortality.[5](#ref-5)–[7](#ref-7) Additional findings that may be supportive of acute right ventricular failure in certain clinical settings include septal straightening or bowing, reflux of contrast in the inferior caval vein, and hepatojugular reflux of contrast into the inferior caval vein. Thrombus load and central location have not shown a consistent association with all-cause mortality.[6](#ref-6)

[![Figure 2](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAIAAAAAAAP///yH5BAEAAAAALAAAAAABAAEAAAIBRAA7)](https://www.ccjm.org/content/ccjom/92/5/301/F2.large.jpg?width=800&height=600&carousel=1 "(A) Computed tomography and (B) echocardiogram showing an increased right ventricle–to–left ventricle ratio, which is used to assess right ventricular strain and dysfunction for risk stratification of pulmonary embolism.")

Echocardiography is invaluable in the assessment of right ventricular dysfunction in acute PE as it can identify numerous findings suggestive of right ventricular dysfunction[5](#ref-5),[7](#ref-7):

* Enlarged right ventricle
* Dilated right ventricle with right ventricle-to-left ventricle ratio (> 1.0)
* McConnell sign (right ventricular free wall akinesis with the apex spared)
* Flattened intraventricular septum
* Distended inferior caval vein with decreased inspiratory collapsibility
* Decreased tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (< 16 mm)
* Decreased peak systolic velocity of tricuspid annulus
* Right heart mobile thrombus or clot in transit
* 60/60 sign (coexistence of acceleration time of pulmonary ejection less than 60 ms and midsystolic notch with mildly elevated [< 60 mm Hg] peak systolic gradient at the tricuspid valve).

Low left ventricular outflow tract velocity time integral of 15 cm or less and right ventricular outflow tract velocity time integral less than 9.5 cm have also been associated with adverse outcomes.[8](#ref-8),[9](#ref-9)

Biomarkers that have been proposed as tools for diagnosis and prognosis of patients with acute PE include troponins (marker of myocardial injury) and natriuretic peptides (marker of right ventricular dysfunction).[7](#ref-7)

## TRIAGING AND RISK STRATIFICATION

Initial management of patients with PE begins with triaging and risk stratification using clinical assessment tools including the Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index (PESI) score or its simplified version (sPESI), cardiac biomarkers, and imaging ([Figure 3](#F3)).[1](#ref-1),[7](#ref-7)

Note the addition of a subcategory of high-risk pulmonary embolism, termed catastrophic pulmonary embolism (those with hemodynamic collapse). Based on information from references 1 and 7.")

Severity of PE and risk of early death are stratified as high, intermediate (intermediate low-risk and intermediate high-risk), and low. Patients classified with high-risk PE are hemodynamically unstable, as defined by cardiac arrest, shock, or hypotension. Patients classified with intermediate-risk PE have signs of right ventricular involvement, while patients classified as low risk do not. Patients with intermediate high-risk PE are hemodynamically stable but have abnormalities in all 3 indicators of risk—clinical (PESI III–V or sPESI ≥ I), laboratory (elevated troponin), and imaging parameters indicative of right ventricular dysfunction (shown on computed tomography pulmonary angiography or echocardiography). Patients classified with intermediate low-risk PE have at least clinically severe presentation and 1 or none of the other parameters.[7](#ref-7) In the registry study noted earlier, the term *catastrophic* PE was introduced as a further classification of patients with high-risk PE and hemodynamic collapse, particularly those requiring vasopressors or experiencing cardiac arrest.[1](#ref-1)

## ESSENTIALS OF MANAGEMENT

Management of PE with right ventricular involvement of varying severity requires prompt, concomitant integration of clinical care focused on hemodynamics (preload and afterload), reperfusion, pharmacologic support, supportive care, and, in refractory cases, use of mechanical circulatory support and advanced therapy ([Table 1](#T1)).[7](#ref-7),[10](#ref-10)

Principles of management options of right ventricular failure in pulmonary embolism

### Preload

Management of preload, particularly fluids and diuresis, has been studied sparsely. In a study of hemodynamically stable patients with submassive PE (defined as a normotensive patient with PE and evidence of right ventricular dysfunction), the cohort receiving intravenous furosemide bolus experienced earlier improvements in parameters of right ventricular function compared with the cohort receiving volume expansion.[11](#ref-11) More recently, in a randomized controlled trial targeting normotensive patients with intermediate-risk PE, a single high-dose bolus of furosemide improved the primary outcomes of normalization of sPESI items and reduced oligoanuria in the first 24 hours (a critical symptom of low cardiac output), and maintained stable renal function compared with placebo.[12](#ref-12) In another trial, right ventricular dysfunction parameters did not differ between patients with intermediate high-risk PE treated with diuresis compared with volume loading; however, diuretics were tolerated safely, and brain-type natriuretic peptide was normalized earlier in the diuretic group.[13](#ref-13)

Although supporting evidence is limited, reducing the preload of an overloaded right ventricle during acute PE with diuresis would be expected to decrease right ventricular load and stress, and fluids could be detrimental. However, if a patient with acute PE has low central venous pressure (by ultrasonography of the inferior caval vein), a modest fluid challenge (≤ 500 mL) may improve the cardiac index.[7](#ref-7) When volume overload is evident, diuresis with concomitant support from vasopressors can be pursued despite hypotension, to target improvement in cardiac output while reducing right ventricular dilation.

### Afterload and reperfusion therapy

Because the thrombus drives the acute increase in right ventricular afterload that is the primary cause of right ventricular dysfunction, it is essential to plan reperfusion early in the course of care.

**High-risk PE**. Primary reperfusion with systemic thrombolysis remains the treatment of choice for patients with high-risk (or massive) PE (defined as syncope, systemic arterial hypotension, cardiogenic shock, or resuscitated cardiac arrest), and, together with anticoagulation initially with unfractionated heparin, readily improves pulmonary vascular resistance, pulmonary artery pressure, and obstruction.[7](#ref-7),[14](#ref-14) Absolute contraindications to intravenous thrombolysis include the following[7](#ref-7):

* A history of hemorrhagic stroke or stroke of unknown origin
* Ischemic stroke in the previous 6 months
* Central nervous system neoplasm
* Major trauma, surgery, or head injury in previous 3 weeks
* Bleeding diathesis
* Active bleeding.

For systemic thrombolysis, lower doses of recombinant tissue–type plasminogen activator (50 mg over 2 hours compared with 100 mg over 2 hours) showed similar efficacy and possibly better safety in patients with acute PE.[15](#ref-15)

The ERS guidelines define the classes of PE treatment recommendations, with surgical embolectomy being recommended (class I indication: evidence or agreement of the benefit of treatment) for patients with high-risk PE who have contraindications to systemic thrombolysis or in whom thrombolysis has failed.[7](#ref-7) Bayiz et al[16](#ref-16) demonstrated the safety and efficacy of percutaneous mechanical aspiration thrombectomy in patients with massive or high-risk PE, who, at follow-up, had decreased pulmonary clot burden and improved hemodynamic parameters, pulmonary artery pressure, right ventricular end-diastolic pressure, and right ventricle-to-left ventricle ratio. Currently, percutaneous catheter-directed treatment is a class IIa indication (weight of evidence favors usefulness of treatment) and should be considered for patients with massive or high-risk PE when thrombolysis is contraindicated or has failed.[7](#ref-7)

**Low- and intermediate-risk PE**. Anticoagulation is recommended (class I indication) for patients with low-to intermediate-risk PE. When oral anticoagulation is initiated, direct oral anticoagulants are preferred over vitamin K antagonists,[7](#ref-7) as these agents have a lower risk of bleeding complications and similar efficacy.[17](#ref-17)

Intermediate-risk (or submassive) PE has been a focus of research in recent years, given the risk for decompensation and subsequent right ventricular strain and dysfunction. Patients with intermediate-risk PE vary in clinical presentation,[1](#ref-1) making management of the clot a crucial part of clinical decision-making. Thrombolysis can prevent hemodynamic decompensation and death in patients with intermediate-risk PE, but it also carries an increased risk of major hemorrhage and stroke.[18](#ref-18) In the PEITHO (Pulmonary Embolism Thrombolysis) trial,[19](#ref-19) thrombolysis in patients with intermediate-risk PE did not affect long-term mortality and did not reduce right ventricular dysfunction or clinical symptoms, compared with anticoagulation alone. In patients with contraindications or in whom thrombolysis has failed, surgical embolectomy was reported to have a high survival rate.[20](#ref-20)

Another modality for thrombus management is placement of an inferior caval vein filter to prevent a clot from reaching the right side of the heart and pulmonary circulation. Routine use of inferior caval vein filters is not recommended, but they should be considered in patients with absolute contraindications to anticoagulation or recurrent PE despite therapeutic anticoagulation.[7](#ref-7)

In conclusion, strategies for reperfusion treatment of intermediate-risk PE remain a gray area. The ERS guidelines[7](#ref-7) determined that anticoagulation is the only class I recommendation for initial treatment of patients with intermediate or high clinical probability of PE. However, promising studies with a focus on emerging techniques are currently taking place.

### Percutaneous interventions for clot management

Catheter-directed therapies have emerged over recent years as safe and effective options.

**Catheter-directed thrombolysis**. In the ULTIMA (Ultrasound Accelerated Thrombolysis of Pulmonary Embolism) trial,[21](#ref-21) ultrasonography-assisted catheter-directed thrombolysis in patients with intermediate-risk PE, in addition to anticoagulation, resulted in reversal of right ventricular dilation and decreased mean right ventricle-to-left ventricle ratio at 24 hours compared with anticoagulation alone, without an increase in bleeding complications.

SEATTLE-II (A Prospective, Single-Arm, Multicenter Trial of EkoSonic Endovascular System and Activase for Treatment of Acute Pulmonary Embolism)[22](#ref-22) studied 150 patients with right ventricular dysfunction (79% had submassive PE and 21% had massive PE) who underwent catheter-directed low-dose fibrinolysis. This therapy resulted in a significant decrease in mean right ventricle-to-left ventricle ratio 48 hours after the procedure (*P* < .0001) and reduced mean pulmonary artery systolic pressure, with a safe bleeding profile and no intracranial hemorrhage at 72 hours.[22](#ref-22) In the OPTALYSE-PE (Optimum Duration of Acoustic Pulse Thrombolysis Procedure in Acute Pulmonary Embolism) trial,[23](#ref-23) catheter-directed therapy with low-dose tissue plasminogen activator administered using a shorter duration of delivery improved clot burden and right ventricular function.

More recent studies have explored outcomes of catheter-directed therapies in patients with intermediate high-risk PE. The CANARY (Catheter-Directed Thrombolysis vs Anticoagulation in Patients With Acute Intermediate-High-Risk Pulmonary Embolism) randomized clinical trial[24](#ref-24) showed significantly lower right ventricle-to-left ventricle ratio at the 3-month echocardiography follow-up after catheter-directed thrombolysis (*P* = .01) compared with anticoagulation monotherapy, although the study was prematurely terminated due to the COVID-19 pandemic. There is an ongoing study comparing catheter-directed thrombolysis vs anticoagulation alone in patients with intermediate high-risk PE.[25](#ref-25)

**Catheter-directed percutaneous mechanical thrombectomy** is an emerging effective treatment option in patients with high- and intermediate-risk PE, without thrombolytic complications and their associated bleeding adverse events. FLARE (FlowTriever Pulmonary Embolectomy Clinical Study)[26](#ref-26) showed significant improvement in the right ventricle-to-left ventricle ratio 48 hours after the procedure, with minimal major bleeding, in patients with intermediate-risk PE. The recent FLAME (FlowTriever for Acute Massive PE) study[27](#ref-27) compared peripheral mechanical thrombectomy with other contemporary therapies (systemic thrombolysis or anticoagulation alone) in patients with high-risk PE and found a lower rate of in-hospital adverse outcomes and 1.9% all-cause mortality in the thrombectomy group. These studies are an important step forward in management options other than systemic thrombolysis for hemodynamically unstable patients with high-risk PE.

Furthermore, a study using data from the largest US National Inpatient Sample database noted that catheter-based therapy (thrombolysis or mechanical thrombectomy) for patients with cancer and intermediate- or high-risk PE was associated with a lower risk of in-hospital mortality or cardiac arrest but had a high risk of bleeding.[28](#ref-28)

In the PERFECT (Pulmonary Embolism Response to Fragmentation, Embolectomy, and Catheter Thrombolysis) multicenter registry,[29](#ref-29) 101 patients with massive (high-risk) and submassive (intermediate high-risk) PE were treated with catheter-directed therapy, including mechanical or pharmacomechanical thrombectomy or thrombolysis. Clinical success—defined as hemodynamic stability, improvement in pulmonary artery pressure and right heart strain, and survival to hospital discharge—was achieved in 85.7% of patients with massive PE and 97.3% of patients with submassive PE. These therapies were found to be safe, with improved right-sided heart function.

## PHARMACOLOGIC SUPPORT

### Inotropes and vasopressors

In patients with high-risk PE and shock, vasopressors are often needed to maintain systemic blood pressure and improve end-organ and coronary perfusion.[7](#ref-7) In cases of persistently low cardiac output despite vasopressor therapy, it is advisable to consider contractility support with inotropes. Norepinephrine and dobutamine are currently recommended as class IIa options for patients with high-risk PE. However, dobutamine should be used cautiously to enhance right ventricular and cardiac output, as it may worsen ventilation-perfusion mismatch and increase the risk of arrhythmias. Additionally, using dobutamine without a vasopressor can exacerbate hypotension.

### Pulmonary vasodilators

The role of pulmonary vasodilation has also been explored in right ventricular dysfunction in patients with PE. In a randomized clinical trial with 20 patients who had acute intermediate high-risk PE, a single-dose of sildenafil (in 10 patients) did not significantly improve the cardiac index and instead lowered blood pressure compared with placebo.[30](#ref-30) In another randomized clinical trial, patients with severe acute submassive (intermediate high-risk) PE who received treatment with nitric oxide did not achieve the primary composite end point of normal right ventricle on echocardiogram and normal plasma troponin T.[31](#ref-31) However, a preplanned post hoc analysis showed that 29% more patients treated with nitric oxide had resolution of right ventricular dilation or hypokinesis at 24 hours.[31](#ref-31) In a randomized clinical trial of 14 patients with acute PE (hemodynamically stable with high clinical probability of right ventricular dysfunction), epoprostenol compared with placebo did not result in improvement of right ventricular dilation or other parameters.[32](#ref-32)

While pulmonary vasodilators can be beneficial in specific types of pulmonary hypertension, their effectiveness in right ventricular failure associated with pulmonary vascular issues may be limited. This is likely due to the unique pathophysiology of PE, particularly the acute increase in afterload resulting from a substantial clot burden. Overall, pulmonary vasodilators are not encouraged, as they can aggravate hypoperfusion of organs and systemic hypotension, despite efforts to decrease blood pressure and pulmonary vascular resistance.[7](#ref-7)

## SUPPORTIVE CARE

For hypoxemic patients, prompt administration of supplemental oxygen therapy is essential. Intubation and mechanical ventilation are reserved for select patients with refractory hypoxemia and unstable hemodynamics, with careful use of anesthetic agents to avoid hypotension and cautious monitoring given the detrimental effects of positive end-expiratory pressure.[7](#ref-7)

In recent years, an integrated approach involving multidisciplinary teams, early risk stratification, and prompt decision-making in patients with intermediate-risk PE has led to lower rates of all-cause mortality,[33](#ref-33) reduced intensive care unit and overall hospital length of stay,[34](#ref-34) and high survival-to-discharge rates.[35](#ref-35) A multidisciplinary team approach in patients with high-risk PE and certain patients with intermediate-risk PE is a class IIa recommendation.[7](#ref-7) In the long term, if patients develop pulmonary hypertension as a complication, referral to a pulmonary hypertension center is highly recommended.

## MECHANICAL CIRCULATORY SUPPORT AND ADVANCED THERAPY

### Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation

Some patients may experience clinical deterioration that is resistant to treatment, including cardiac arrest or worsening hemodynamic shock requiring increased vasopressor support. In these cases, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) can be used as a bridging or rescue therapy; the ERS classified this as a class IIb recommendation (efficacy of treatment is less well established).[7](#ref-7) Venoarterial ECMO can bypass blocked pulmonary circulation by providing sufficient cardiac output to sustain systemic and coronary blood flow until the thrombus is effectively managed. However, using ECMO for an extended period, typically more than 5 to 10 days, can result in complications.[7](#ref-7)

Another detailed analysis from the National Inpatient Sample database of patients with high-risk PE revealed that use of ECMO in patients with massive PE increased from 0.07% to 1.1% from 2005 to 2013 and its use was not associated with a change in in-hospital mortality (61.6%).[36](#ref-36) ECMO was performed in 0.3% of hospitalized patients with high-risk PE for a duration of 1.9 ± 4.1 days from the index admission date, and the median hospital length of stay was 10 days. In patients with high-risk PE using ECMO for hemodynamic support, independent predictors of mortality included age, female sex, obesity, congestive heart failure, and chronic pulmonary disease.[36](#ref-36)

A handful of studies have looked at using ECMO as a bridge to ultimate clot management in patients with high-risk PE. In a cohort of 20 patients with high-risk PE who were managed with venoarterial ECMO for a median 5.1 days, 94.7% had normal right ventricular function at discharge.[37](#ref-37) Another group of 16 patients with acute high-risk PE, 12 of whom were in cardiac arrest, underwent venoarterial ECMO for a mean duration of 1.5 days and had an overall 30-day mortality rate of 43.8%; treatment was mainly with ECMO alone, ECMO with thrombolysis, and ECMO with embolectomy.[38](#ref-38) While a meta-analysis on venoarterial ECMO and acute massive PE did not show significantly different in-hospital mortality between patients treated with or without ECMO,[39](#ref-39) another meta-analysis of venoarterial ECMO showed low-quality evidence of higher survival rates in patients 60 years or younger and in those who underwent surgical embolectomy.[40](#ref-40) There was evidence that venoarterial ECMO improves short-term survival of patients with acute PE.[40](#ref-40)

The 2022 American Heart Association guidelines maintain their earlier statement on cardiopulmonary resuscitation, which suggests that extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation for cardiac arrest from PE can be considered as a bridge to reperfusion therapy in select patients when it can be implemented and conventional cardiopulmonary resuscitation is failing.[41](#ref-41)

### Right ventricular assist devices

Right ventricular assist devices have been explored for refractory shock related to PE. The devices can be placed surgically, with cannulation performed in the right atrium or right ventricle and pulmonary artery while connected with an extracorporeal flow pump.[4](#ref-4) They also can be placed percutaneously with lower flow than surgical right ventricular assist devices. Right ventricular assist devices, while offloading the right atrium and right ventricle from excessive preload, ultimately increase right ventricular afterload by generating constant flow and pressure in the pulmonary artery.[4](#ref-4) The percutaneous right ventricular assist device Impella RP, when used in hemodynamically unstable patients with PE, can lead to shock reversal with improvement in cardiac index and hemodynamic stability.[10](#ref-10)

Overall, there is a lack of sufficient evidence on outcomes of patients with acute high-risk PE undergoing treatment with ECMO, Impella RP, or other right ventricular assist devices. The decision to bridge with mechanical circulatory support should be made on a case-by-case basis, using a multidisciplinary team approach that involves intensivists, cardiologists with expertise in heart failure, pulmonologists, and cardiothoracic surgeons.

## CONCLUSION

The incidence and burden of PE have risen in recent decades. Mortality, particularly in patients at high-risk with significant right ventricular involvement, is alarmingly high. An integrated approach to risk stratification and prompt implementation of therapies are critical to manage acute, life-threatening and long-term sequelae of PE, given PE’s relationship with right-sided heart dysfunction. There are evidence gaps in the management of right ventricular failure due to PE, and further studies are warranted to aid in decision-making.

results.content: In patients with intermediate-high-risk pulmonary embolism (PE; ie, biochemical and imaging evidence of right ventricle [RV] dysfunction), catheter-directed embolectomy is commonly performed but has not been compared with anticoagulation alone. In a recent randomized trial of 100 such patients, suction embolectomy followed by anticoagulation did not improve mortality but did result in a greater reduction of the right ventricular (RV)/left ventricular (LV) ratio (an indicator of RV strain) compared with anticoagulation alone (0.52 versus 0.24) . In addition, normalization of tachycardia and indicators of pulmonary artery obstruction improved in a larger proportion of patients undergoing embolectomy. The adverse event rate (including bleeding) was similar between the groups, as was the need [...] AHA/ACC guidelines for pulmonary embolism (March 2026)

ADULT RESUSCITATION

Catheter-directed thrombolysis versus anticoagulation in pulmonary embolism (March 2026)

In patients with intermediate-high-risk pulmonary embolism (PE; ie, biochemical and imaging evidence of right ventricle [RV] dysfunction), limited data suggest that catheter-directed thrombolysis improves RV function compared with anticoagulation alone, but does not improve mortality. In a recent randomized trial of 544 patients with intermediate-high-risk PE, ultrasound-facilitated, catheter-directed thrombolysis with [alteplase](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/alteplase-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) reduced the composite outcome of PE-related death, cardiorespiratory decompensation, or symptomatic PE recurrence compared with anticoagulation alone (4 versus 10 percent); this difference was driven primarily by fewer episodes of decompensation (3.7 versus 10.3 percent) [[1](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/1)]. Major bleeding was numerically higher in the alteplase group (4 versus 2 percent) but was not statistically significant, and the difference in RV size at 48 hours between the two groups was also not significant. Interpretation is limited by low event rates, lack of blinding, and underrepresentation of patients >75 years. However, these data support our practice of performing catheter-directed therapies in patients with intermediate-high-risk PE. (See ["Acute pulmonary embolism in adults: Reperfusion therapy in intermediate- and high-risk patients", section on 'Catheter-directed thrombolysis'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/acute-pulmonary-embolism-in-adults-reperfusion-therapy-in-intermediate-and-high-risk-patients?sectionName=Catheter-directed+thrombolysis&topicRef=8365&anchor=H4140125415&source=see_link#H4140125415).)

Updated international Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines (March 2026)

The Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines have recently been updated [[2](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/2)]. The guidelines suggested that, while a mean arterial pressure of 65 mmHg should be targeted, a range of 60 to 70 mmHg is practical for most adults with sepsis. The guidelines also emphasized the importance of screening tools for early detection and management of sepsis, while discouraging both overly aggressive fluid resuscitation and empiric treatment for fungal and anaerobic bacterial infections, especially when suspicion is low. The guidelines encouraged active fluid removal (in the later phases of shock), rapid de-escalation of antimicrobials and, in mechanically ventilated patients, the use of selective digestive tract decontamination to prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia. We agree with these recommendations. (See ["Evaluation and management of suspected sepsis and septic shock in adults", section on 'Introduction'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/evaluation-and-management-of-suspected-sepsis-and-septic-shock-in-adults?sectionName=INTRODUCTION&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1&source=see_link#H1).)

Joint European and United States definition of refractory septic shock (March 2026)

Although sepsis and septic shock have widely accepted definitions, there has not been consensus regarding the definition of "refractory" septic shock. The Society of Critical Care Medicine and European Society of Intensive Care Medicine have recently proposed criteria defining refractory septic shock by the presence of (1) persistently elevated lactate concentration (>2 mmol/L [>18 mg/dL]) and/or prolonged capillary refill time, (2) lack of response to fluid resuscitation, (3) a norepinephrine base equivalent dose >0.5 micrograms per kilogram per minute, and (4) in those with suspected mixed shock, critical care ultrasound should be used to confirm lack of response to fluids and to exclude other etiologies for shock [[3](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/3)]. The impact of this definition on patient outcomes, such as survival, remains undetermined. (See ["Sepsis syndromes in adults: Epidemiology, definitions, clinical presentation, diagnosis, and prognosis", section on 'Septic shock'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/sepsis-syndromes-in-adults-epidemiology-definitions-clinical-presentation-diagnosis-and-prognosis?sectionName=Septic+shock&topicRef=8365&anchor=H8&source=see_link#H8).)

High-flow oxygen does not affect mortality in hypoxemic respiratory failure (March 2026)

Although frequently used, the value of high-flow oxygen delivered via nasal cannulae (HFNC) in patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure remains unclear. In a randomized trial of 1110 such patients, HFNC did not reduce 28-day mortality compared with low-flow oxygen [[4](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/4)]. HFNC led to a non-significant reduction in the intubation rate at 28 days (42.4 versus 48.4 percent), and rapidly improved patients' respiratory rates, dyspnea, and carbon dioxide levels. These data support our practice of administering HFNC only to patients with advanced oxygen needs (eg, >6 L/minute) rather than routine administration. (See ["Evaluation and management of the nonventilated, hospitalized adult patient with acute hypoxemia", section on 'Humidified, high-flow oxygen delivered via nasal cannulae (HFNC)'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/evaluation-and-management-of-the-nonventilated-hospitalized-adult-patient-with-acute-hypoxemia?sectionName=Humidified%2C+high-flow+oxygen+delivered+via+nasal+cannulae+%28HFNC%29&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3611214250&source=see_link#H3611214250).)

Updated resuscitation guidelines for adults (January 2026)

The American Heart Association and European Resuscitation Council have published updated guidelines for adult cardiopulmonary resuscitation and emergency care [[5,6](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/5,6)]. Resuscitation updates include: urgent electrical cardioversion for patients who are unstable and those with rate-related ischemia caused by atrial fibrillation or flutter; immediate defibrillation for all adult patients with sustained polymorphic ventricular tachycardia; and increased support for using extracorporeal devices for potentially reversible causes of cardiac arrest where resources are available. Post-resuscitation updates include a normocapnic ventilation target and recommendations for a target temperature ≤37.5°C for a minimum of 36 hours following return of spontaneous circulation. (See ["Advanced cardiac life support (ACLS) in adults", section on 'Management of specific arrhythmias'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/advanced-cardiac-life-support-acls-in-adults?sectionName=MANAGEMENT+OF+SPECIFIC+ARRHYTHMIAS&topicRef=8365&anchor=H7&source=see_link#H7) and ["Intensive care unit management of the intubated post-cardiac arrest adult patient", section on 'Setting the target temperature'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/intensive-care-unit-management-of-the-intubated-post-cardiac-arrest-adult-patient?sectionName=Setting+the+target+temperature&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1286775785&source=see_link#H1286775785).)

Induction and tracheal intubation in critically ill patients using etomidate or ketamine (December 2025)

Concern exists regarding induction with [etomidate](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/etomidate-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) during rapid sequence intubation (RSI) in critically ill patients, particularly septic patients, because of transient adrenocortical suppression that may worsen outcomes. [Ketamine](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/ketamine-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) has been proposed as an alternative for such patients, but it stimulates catecholamine release and may increase risk of myocardial ischemia or pulmonary hypertension. A pragmatic trial of more than 2300 critically ill adults undergoing RSI in the emergency department or intensive care unit found similar in-hospital 28-day mortality between the ketamine and etomidate groups (28 versus 29 percent) [[7](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/7)]. Almost half of the patients had sepsis or septic shock, also with no difference in mortality (39 versus 38 percent). These findings suggest that either etomidate or ketamine is a reasonable induction agent in critically ill patients, including those with sepsis. (See ["General anesthesia: Intravenous induction agents", section on 'Disadvantages and adverse effects'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/general-anesthesia-intravenous-induction-agents?sectionName=Disadvantages+and+adverse+effects&topicRef=8365&anchor=H262499028&source=see_link#H262499028).)

Updated sequential organ failure assessment score (SOFA-2) (December 2025)

An updated Sepsis Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score, termed SOFA-2, has been published [[8](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/8)]. SOFA-2 resolves many of the deficiencies of SOFA-1 (eg, inclusion of a broader range of organ failure thresholds in the original six organ domains). Data from over 2 million patients in over 1300 intensive care units (ICUs) were used to develop and validate the score in all-comer ICU patients. SOFA-2 and SOFA-1 demonstrated a similar ability to predict ICU mortality. A 1-point increase in SOFA-2 increased the odds of ICU mortality (odds ratio, 1.378). Sequential SOFA-2 calculations from ICU day 1 to 7 remained predictive throughout those seven days. We agree with the updated version of SOFA; however, it does not automatically change the SOFA-1-based Sepsis-3 definition for sepsis and septic shock. (See ["Predictive scoring systems in the intensive care unit", section on 'Sequential (sepsis-related) Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA)'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/predictive-scoring-systems-in-the-intensive-care-unit?sectionName=Sequential+%28sepsis-related%29+Organ+Failure+Assessment+%28SOFA%29&topicRef=8365&anchor=H889841588&source=see_link#H889841588).)

Arterial catheter in shock (December 2025)

Whether an arterial catheter should be routinely inserted in patients with shock is unclear. A recent trial reported outcomes comparing arterial catheter placement with no catheter in over 1000 patients with shock, half of whom had sepsis [[9](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/9)]. Ninety-day mortality was similar between the two groups (34 versus 37 percent). Pain, hemorrhage, and hematoma were more common in the arterial catheter group. Limitations of the study include a lack of blinding, baseline group differences, and limited applicability to specific types of shock. Nonetheless, these results suggest that many patients can be managed without an arterial catheter, although our approach is to place an arterial catheter when a reasonable indication is present (eg, labile blood pressure, unreliable blood pressure readings). (See ["Evaluation and management of suspected sepsis and septic shock in adults", section on 'Monitoring catheters'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/evaluation-and-management-of-suspected-sepsis-and-septic-shock-in-adults?sectionName=Monitoring+catheters&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3514478798&source=see_link#H3514478798).)

Capillary refill time as a tissue perfusion biomarker in septic shock (December 2025)

Preliminary data suggest that using capillary refill time (CRT) as a clinical biomarker of tissue perfusion may lower mortality in patients with septic shock. In a recent trial, a protocol that used CRT to tailor fluid, vasopressor, and inotrope therapy was compared with usual care in over 1500 patients with early septic shock [[10](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/10)]. The CRT protocol reduced the duration of vital organ support by 5 percent. The CRT group also received less fluid and had a higher percentage of patients receiving vasopressor therapy. However, mortality was similar, the trial was unblinded, and the impact of the additional components of the CRT protocol on outcomes was not accurately assessed. Nonetheless, these data support our practice of including CRT as part of the bedside assessment when monitoring the response to therapy in patients with septic shock. (See ["Evaluation and management of suspected sepsis and septic shock in adults", section on 'Clinical'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/evaluation-and-management-of-suspected-sepsis-and-septic-shock-in-adults?sectionName=Clinical&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1643153952&source=see_link#H1643153952).)

Tracheoarterial fistula: A large series description (December 2025)

Tracheoarterial fistula is a late, life-threatening complication of tracheostomy placement associated with high mortality. In a series date of almost 150 patients, the median time to fistula development was 80 days [[11](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/11)]. Only half of patients had the classic feature of an initial small "sentinel" bleed followed by massive hemorrhage a few hours or days later. Imaging (typically computed tomography) was better at diagnosing the fistula than bronchoscopy (80 versus 32 percent). Tracheostomy cuff overinflation and sternal notch pressure controlled the bleeding in over 70 percent of patients while waiting for definitive therapy (ie, endovascular or surgical repair). These data inform early recognition, diagnosis, and treatment of the most fatal complication of tracheostomy. (See ["Tracheostomy: Postoperative care, maintenance, and complications in adults", section on 'Tracheoarterial fistula'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/tracheostomy-postoperative-care-maintenance-and-complications-in-adults?sectionName=Tracheoarterial+fistula&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3292466807&source=see_link#H3292466807).)

Energy selection for cardioversion of atrial fibrillation (November 2025)

Energy settings for cardioversion of atrial fibrillation (AF) have evolved. Earlier major society guidelines recommended using lower energies based upon concern that higher energies might increase the risk of cardiac injury and other complications. The 2025 American Heart Association Adult Advanced Life Support guidelines recommend 200 J initial energy selection for cardioversion of AF based upon results of randomized trials demonstrating >90 percent cumulative cardioversion success with 200 J with biphasic defibrillators and lower risk of provoking ventricular fibrillation with cardioversion using ≥200 J than with low-energy monophasic shocks [[5](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/5)]. (See ["Cardioversion and defibrillation for specific arrhythmias", section on 'Waveform and energy selection'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/cardioversion-and-defibrillation-for-specific-arrhythmias?sectionName=Waveform+and+energy+selection&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2562597&source=see_link#H2562597).)

ENVIRONMENTAL EMERGENCIES

Iloprost for amputation prevention in frostbite (May 2026)

[Iloprost](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/iloprost-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) is a prostacyclin analog that is indicated for the treatment of grade 3 or 4 frostbite (ie, cyanosis that extends proximal to the distal phalanx after rewarming), but supporting evidence is limited. In a study with over 250 patients (80 receiving iloprost) in two Canadian regions that differed in routine iloprost use but with a standardized frostbite care pathway, iloprost was associated with a lower amputation rate for grade 3 frostbite (30 versus 53 percent) but not for grade 2 and 4 frostbite; patients receiving a higher total iloprost dose were less likely to have amputations [[12](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/12)]. In 40 patients with grade 4 frostbite, iloprost treatment was associated with fewer finger and toe segment amputations (40 versus 51 percent and 47 versus 58 percent, respectively). These findings support our recommendation for iloprost in patients with severe frostbite. (See ["Frostbite: Acute care and prevention", section on 'Iloprost within 72 hours'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/frostbite-acute-care-and-prevention?sectionName=Iloprost+within+72+hours&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1902794625&source=see_link#H1902794625).)

Microorganisms in children with freshwater drowning-associated pneumonia (February 2026)

Infection with gram-negative organisms, especially _Aeromonas_ species, is predominantly reported in patients with drowning-associated pneumonia (DAP). In a study from China of over 70 children with freshwater DAP in a pediatric intensive care unit, _Staphylococcus aureus_ was the most isolated organism [[13](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/13)]. Other common pathogens included _Mycoplasma pneumoniae_, _Streptococcus pneumoniae_, _Haemophilus influenzae_, _Klebsiella pneumoniae_, _Candida albicans_, and rhinovirus. These findings highlight the need for an empiric broad-spectrum antibiotic regimen, including coverage of gram-positive bacteria, in children with suspected DAP. (See ["Drowning (submersion injuries)", section on 'Pneumonia'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/drowning-submersion-injuries?sectionName=Pneumonia&topicRef=8365&anchor=H809358478&source=see_link#H809358478).)

Effectiveness of defibrillation in patients with hypothermia and nonperfusing shockable rhythm (February 2026)

Patients with hypothermia and nonperfusing shockable arrhythmias are less likely to have return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) with defibrillation at a core temperature <30°C (86°F). Current recommendations are to attempt defibrillation with up to three shocks but withhold further attempts pending rewarming since cold myocardium can potentially be injured. A registry-based study with almost 40 patients with cardiac arrest, a shockable rhythm, and core temperature <30°C found that ROSC was more likely if defibrillation was performed during rewarming, as compared with before rewarming (100 versus 25 percent) [[14](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/14)]. Defibrillation during extracorporeal life support (ECLS) had a fivefold increase in odds of ROSC. These findings support our recommendations to attempt defibrillation even with temperature <30°C and to not withhold defibrillation during ECLS rewarming at temperature >25°C (77°F). (See ["Accidental hypothermia in adults: Management", section on 'Ventricular arrhythmias or asystole'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/accidental-hypothermia-in-adults-management?sectionName=Ventricular+arrhythmias+or+asystole&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1808505299&source=see_link#H1808505299).)

Acute hypersensitivity reactions from rattlesnake antivenom in alpha-gal endemic region (February 2026)

CroFab and Anavip, antivenoms used to treat Crotalinae snakebite envenomation, can potentially cause severe allergic reactions. Anavip contains more of the carbohydrate moiety galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose (which is responsible for alpha-gal syndrome) compared with CroFab. A study with over 200 patients in Arkansas (a state with a high rate of alpha-gal sensitization) who received either Anavip or CroFab found that Anavip was associated with increased adverse drug reactions (including presumed anaphylaxis) compared with CroFab (22 versus 4 percent) [[15](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/15)]. Basophil activation testing from individuals with known alpha-gal syndrome found that Anavip more potently activated alpha-gal sensitized basophils. Clinicians who treat snakebite victims in regions with high rates of alpha-gal sensitization must be ready to manage anaphylaxis following antivenom (especially Anavip) administration. (See ["Bites by Crotalinae snakes (rattlesnakes, cottonmouths [water moccasins], or copperheads) in the United States: Management", section on 'Acute antivenom hypersensitivity reactions'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/bites-by-crotalinae-snakes-rattlesnakes-cottonmouths-water-moccasins-or-copperheads-in-the-united-states-management?sectionName=Acute+antivenom+hypersensitivity+reactions&topicRef=8365&anchor=H4098260420&source=see_link#H4098260420).)

GENERAL ADULT EMERGENCY MEDICINE

Fosphenytoin for trigeminal neuralgia attacks (May 2026)

Several pharmacologic options are available to treat acute trigeminal neuralgia (TN) pain, but available supporting evidence is limited. In a randomized trial that included 22 patients with acute TN symptoms, pain reduction on the numerical rating scale (0 for no pain up to 10 for worst pain) was greater at two hours among those assigned to [fosphenytoin](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/fosphenytoin-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) than placebo (-6.1 versus -2.4) [[16](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/16)]. Treatment consisted of a loading dose followed by once daily maintenance treatment for up to four days. Patients assigned to fosphenytoin also had a higher rate of >50 percent pain reduction and reduction in the frequency of attack recurrence, and treatment was generally well tolerated. These data provide clinical trial evidence to support the role of fosphenytoin for acute TN exacerbations. (See ["Trigeminal neuralgia", section on 'Acute rescue therapy for patients with breakthrough pain'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/trigeminal-neuralgia?sectionName=Acute+rescue+therapy+for+patients+with+breakthrough+pain&topicRef=8365&anchor=H372586115&source=see_link#H372586115).)

AHA/ACC guidelines for pulmonary embolism (March 2026)

Several societies, including the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC), have issued joint guidelines for the evaluation and management of pulmonary embolism (PE) [[17](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/17)]. The guidelines stratify patients by risk of PE-related death to facilitate management. Patients in category A (incidental PE), B (symptomatic PE with a low clinical severity score), and C (symptomatic PE with an elevated clinical severity score) require anticoagulation. Patients in category D (incipient cardiopulmonary failure) and E (cardiopulmonary failure) are candidates for reperfusion therapies (eg, thrombectomy or thrombolysis, if they have a low bleeding risk). We await adoption of this classification and encourage its use to facilitate management. (See ["Acute pulmonary embolism in adults: Treatment overview and prognosis", section on 'American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology/others'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/acute-pulmonary-embolism-in-adults-treatment-overview-and-prognosis?sectionName=American+Heart+Association%2FAmerican+College+of+Cardiology%2Fothers&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2148862999&source=see_link#H2148862999).)

Age-adjusted D-dimer cutoffs in deep vein thrombosis diagnosis (January 2026)

D-dimer values rise with age, decreasing specificity in older patients when a fixed cutoff is used to diagnose deep venous thrombosis (DVT). In a study of 2169 patients with low to moderate pretest probability for DVT, using an age-adjusted D-dimer (age [years] x 10 ng/mL for patients >50 years) compared with a fixed conventional cutoff of 500 ng/mL resulted in a 7 percent absolute increase in patients for whom DVT was excluded without lower extremity compression ultrasonography [[18](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/18)]. At three months, there were no VTE events in patients with a D-dimer level ≥500 ng/mL but below the age-adjusted cutoff. These data strengthen the case for more widespread utilization of age-adjusted D-dimer to diagnose DVT in older adults. (See ["Clinical presentation and diagnosis of the nonpregnant adult with suspected deep vein thrombosis of the lower extremity", section on 'Adjusted cutoffs'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/clinical-presentation-and-diagnosis-of-the-nonpregnant-adult-with-suspected-deep-vein-thrombosis-of-the-lower-extremity?sectionName=Adjusted+cutoffs&topicRef=8365&anchor=H410968138&source=see_link#H410968138).)

Andexanet alfa removed from the United States market (January 2026)

[Andexanet alfa](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/andexanet-alfa-inactivated-coagulation-factor-xa-recombinant-united-states-withdrawn-from-market-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link), a specific reversal agent for factor Xa inhibitors that was approved in 2018, has been removed from the United States market, as reported in a communication from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) [[19](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/19)]. The communication mentions concerns about an increased rate of serious thrombotic complications compared with usual care in the ANNEXA-I trial and states that the company has voluntarily withdrawn the licensing application for commercial reasons. For life-threatening bleeding associated with factor Xa inhibitors, 4-factor unactivated prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) can be used along with other hemostatic measures. (See ["Management of bleeding in patients receiving direct oral anticoagulants", section on 'Andexanet alfa'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/management-of-bleeding-in-patients-receiving-direct-oral-anticoagulants?sectionName=Andexanet+alfa&topicRef=8365&anchor=H635532401&source=see_link#H635532401) and ["Hemostatic treatments for anticoagulated patients with intracranial hemorrhage", section on 'Andexanet alfa if PCC is unavailable'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/hemostatic-treatments-for-anticoagulated-patients-with-intracranial-hemorrhage?sectionName=Andexanet+alfa+if+PCC+is+unavailable&topicRef=8365&anchor=H4272016095&source=see_link#H4272016095).)

Suction embolectomy versus anticoagulation in pulmonary embolism (January 2026)

In patients with intermediate-high-risk pulmonary embolism (PE; ie, biochemical and imaging evidence of right ventricle [RV] dysfunction), catheter-directed embolectomy is commonly performed but has not been compared with anticoagulation alone. In a recent randomized trial of 100 such patients, suction embolectomy followed by anticoagulation did not improve mortality but did result in a greater reduction of the right ventricular (RV)/left ventricular (LV) ratio (an indicator of RV strain) compared with anticoagulation alone (0.52 versus 0.24) [[20](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/20)]. In addition, normalization of tachycardia and indicators of pulmonary artery obstruction improved in a larger proportion of patients undergoing embolectomy. The adverse event rate (including bleeding) was similar between the groups, as was the need for intensive care unit admission and hospital length of stay; PE did not recur in either group. This study provides additional support for the use of catheter-directed embolectomy in patients with intermediate-high-risk PE with the goal of faster thrombus resolution and reduction in RV load. (See ["Acute pulmonary embolism in adults: Reperfusion therapy in intermediate- and high-risk patients", section on 'Suction/mechanical embolectomy'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/acute-pulmonary-embolism-in-adults-reperfusion-therapy-in-intermediate-and-high-risk-patients?sectionName=Suction%2Fmechanical+embolectomy&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3973928105&source=see_link#H3973928105).)

Post-thoracentesis ultrasonography for residual fluid evaluation (December 2025)

With the routine use of lung ultrasonography for therapeutic thoracentesis, it is unclear whether post-procedure chest radiography to still necessary to assess for residual fluid. In a recent prospective study of 147 patients with a free-flowing pleural effusion, there was excellent agreement between lung ultrasonography (performed immediately after the procedure) and chest radiography (performed four hours after thoracentesis; Gwet's agreement coefficient 0.93) [[21](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/21)]. There was also strong agreement between the proceduralist's interpretation and that of the blind ultrasound reviewer (kappa 0.81). These results suggest that ultrasonography is sufficient for evaluating residual fluid after thoracentesis; however, these findings may not be generalizable to patients with trapped lung and need additional study. (See ["Ultrasound-guided thoracentesis", section on 'Follow-up'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/ultrasound-guided-thoracentesis?sectionName=FOLLOW-UP&topicRef=8365&anchor=H9&source=see_link#H9).)
